summary: Given n distinct numbers from [0, n], return the one value of that range that is missing.
mainInsight: The full range 0..n has a known total n(n+1)/2 (or a known XOR), so the missing value is that total minus the actual sum, with O(1) extra space.
invariant: For the XOR version, after processing index i the accumulator is the XOR of 0..i+1 and nums[0..i], so all present values cancel in pairs.

approaches.name: Sort and scan
approaches.summary: Sort, then return the first index i with nums[i] != i (or n).
approaches.spaceComplexity: O(1) to O(n) depending on sort

approaches.name: Hash set
approaches.summary: Put all values in a set, then check 0..n.
approaches.interviewRelevance: Fine first answer, misses the follow-up.

approaches.name: XOR
approaches.summary: XOR all indices 0..n and all values; pairs cancel and the missing value remains.
approaches.interviewRelevance: Equally good; mention for the overflow argument.

commonMistakes: Using n - 1 instead of n as the top of the range (the range is 0..n, which has n + 1 values).
Forgetting that the missing value can be n itself or 0.
Integer overflow of the sum in Java/C++ (use XOR or long).

cards.answer: Gauss sum of 0..n minus the actual sum. Clue: The array holds n distinct numbers from the range [0, n], so exactly one value of a complete, known range is absent.
keyPoints: The array holds n distinct numbers from the range [0, n], so exactly one value of a complete, known range is absent.
cards.explanation: When the full set is known, an aggregate of it (sum or XOR) minus the same aggregate of what you have isolates the missing element.

rubric.technique: Gauss sum of 0..n minus the actual sum
aliases: xor of all indices and values

alsoValid.note: correct but uses linear extra space

alsoValid.note: correct but sorting costs n log n

rubric.clue: The array holds n distinct numbers from the range [0, n], so exactly one value of a complete, known range is absent.

promptVariants: What does the function return for nums = [1]?
cards.explanation: n = 1, so the range is [0, 1]. Expected sum 1 minus actual sum 1 = 0.

incorrectOptionExplanations.1: 1 is present; the missing value is 0.
incorrectOptionExplanations.-1: Exactly one value is always missing; there is no not-found case.

promptVariants: The expected sum of the range 0..n is n * (n ___ 1) // 2.
cards.explanation: The range has n + 1 values 0..n; their sum is n(n+1)/2. Using n - 1 sums only 0..n-1 and misses the case where n is missing.

promptVariants: Why might an interviewer prefer the XOR version over the sum in Java?
What advantage does XOR-ing indices and values have over the sum formula?
options: XOR cannot overflow; the sum can exceed int32
XOR runs in O(log n) time instead of O(n)
XOR also works when two numbers are missing
XOR does not need to know n
cards.answer: XOR cannot overflow; the sum can exceed int32
cards.explanation: x ^ x = 0 cancels every present value against its index, leaving the missing one, and XOR never grows beyond the bit width.

incorrectOptionExplanations.XOR runs in O(log n) time instead of O(n: Both read every element once: O(n).
incorrectOptionExplanations.XOR also works when two numbers are miss: With two missing you get a ^ b, which needs extra work to split.
incorrectOptionExplanations.XOR does not need to know n: XOR also includes n (or uses len(nums)), just like the sum.

promptVariants: Why is a hash set not the answer to the follow-up?

options: It needs O(n) extra space, not O(1)
Set lookups are O(log n), making it O(n log n)

It fails when the missing number is n
cards.answer: It needs O(n) extra space, not O(1)
cards.explanation: The follow-up asks for O(n) time and O(1) extra space; the sum and XOR tricks meet both.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Set lookups are O(log n), making it O(n: Hash set lookups are O(1) on average.
